The Australian spotted mackerel (Scomberomorus munroi) attains a maximum recorded fork length of 104 centimeters [Li = 104 centimeters], placing it among the larger members of the genus that inhabit tropical and subtropical waters. Females first reach reproductive maturity at a considerably smaller size, with the fork length at puberty documented at 61 centimeters [Lp = 61 centimeters], a threshold that signals the onset of gonadal development and the capacity to contribute to spawning aggregations. Field surveys conducted across the species' range in northern Australian waters have confirmed that individuals begin participating in spawning events once they surpass this size, which typically corresponds to an age of several years. The length-based maturation schedule observed in Scomberomorus munroi aligns with patterns reported for congeneric species such as Scomberomorus brasiliensis and Scomberomorus maculatus, suggesting a conserved relationship between body size and reproductive ontogeny within the genus. Comparative analyses of length-at-age data indicate that the species invests substantially in somatic growth before diverting resources toward gamete production, a life-history strategy that buffers against environmental variability in prey availability.

The spawning season extends over several months, allowing females to release multiple batches of eggs that contribute to the overall annual reproductive effort. Field observations indicate that the species is an iteroparous broadcast spawner, releasing buoyant, fertilized ova directly into the water column where they undergo external development.

The ecological role of Scomberomorus munroi as a highly mobile, pelagic predator influences its distribution and habitat use across the continental shelf of northern Australia. Juvenile individuals, after completing their pelagic larval phase and undergoing metamorphosis, recruit to nearshore environments where they exploit abundant prey resources to fuel their rapid somatic growth. As they mature and increase in both length and mass, sub-adults shift to deeper, offshore waters where they join adult spawning aggregations.
